Void fraction (ϕ=Vgas​/Vmixture​)

Words: 177 Articles: 2
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
The void fraction is the fraction of a mixture's local volume occupied by gas. For a horizontally uniform bubbly liquid it is the transported concentration in a one-dimensional gas-volume continuity equation. It is distinct from gas mass fraction because gas and liquid have different mass densities.

Kinematic bubble transport in an exponentially narrowing vessel (ϕt​+Vs​(1−2ϕ)ϕz​=2βVs​ϕ(1−ϕ))

Words: 72
Void fraction OurBigBook.com
If the vessel radius is proportional to e−βz, its area is proportional to e−2βz. Gas-volume conservation gives the displayed equation. Along concentration characteristic curves, z˙=Vs​(1−2ϕ) and ϕ˙​=2βVs​ϕ(1−ϕ). Uniform initial concentration stays uniform in the uninterrupted bubbly region and follows this logistic law. Individual bubbles move at Vs​(1−ϕ) instead: their rise distance there is η=−(2β)−1log[ϕ0​+(1−ϕ0​)e−2βVs​t]. Boundary interactions and dense-mixture backflow can invalidate the simplified closure.

Bubble clearing in a cylindrical vessel (Φ(t)=ϕ0​[1−Vs​(1−ϕ0​)t/H]+​)

Words: 63
Void fraction OurBigBook.com
For initially uniform bubbles with upward speed Vs​(1−ϕ), no new gas production and free escape at the top, gas conservation gives flux Vs​ϕ(1−ϕ). A clearing shock rises from the impermeable bottom with speed Vs​(1−ϕ0​) by the Rankine-Hugoniot condition. The displayed mean void fraction averages the remaining uniform region over the whole liquid depth H. This assumes the dilute regime and no retained foam layer.

Strouhal number (St=ωh/U)

Words: 49
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
The Strouhal number compares the advective time h/U with a prescribed forcing time 1/ω. Some conventions use ordinary frequency instead of angular frequency, introducing a factor 2π. For a longitudinal disturbance extending over length λh, the relevant ratio is λSt rather than St alone.

Lift (force)

Words: 41
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Lift is the component of the fluid force on a body perpendicular to its far-field relative velocity; the parallel component is drag. In a two-dimensional ideal circulatory flow, the Kutta–Joukowski theorem gives the lift per unit span from the far-field speed and circulation.

Airfoil

Words: 27
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An airfoil is a body profile designed to generate lift in a surrounding flow. In two-dimensional potential flow, its circulation-dependent lift per unit span is described by the Kutta–Joukowski theorem.

Uniform flow (u(x)=U)

Words: 36
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A uniform flow has the same velocity at every position. A constant velocity field has zero divergence and zero vorticity; a velocity potential is ϕ(x)=U⋅x. It describes the remote ambient flow in idealized obstacle and line vortex problems.

Volume viscosity (ζB​)

Words: 62
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Bulk viscosity is the dissipative response to a fluid's volume expansion or compression, distinct from the shear response. For a Newtonian isotropic fluid its isotropic dissipative stress includes ζB​(∇⋅v)I, and nonnegative ζB​ gives nonnegative compression-related dissipation. A condensate's relative-density-flow bulk coefficient must be identified from its particular hydrodynamic equation; it is not automatically numerically identical to a dimensional Newtonian viscosity.

Hydraulic resistance (R=Δp/Q)

Words: 63
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Hydraulic resistance relates the pressure drop across a resistive fluid element to its volumetric flow rate. In a linear model, Δp=RQ with R>0, so dissipated mechanical power is ΔpQ=RQ2. A peripheral circulatory bed can be represented by such a resistance when its detailed dynamics are not retained. This terminal pressure-to-flow resistance differs from the area-dependent friction rate multiplying velocity in a distributed tube momentum equation.

Physiological fluid dynamics

Words: 1k Articles: 24
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Physiological fluid dynamics studies the motion of fluids in biological systems, including blood flow in elastic arteries, flow through deformable vessels, and liquid layers lining airways. Wall compliance couples pressure to geometry, so wave propagation and mechanical feedback are as important as viscosity.

Lubrication model of a compliant translating plug (px​=−6μU/h2+12μQ/h3)

Words: 190 Articles: 2
Physiological fluid dynamics OurBigBook.com
For a freely translating compliant body separated from a cylindrical wall by a thin lubrication gap h, the body frame has wall speed −U and body surface speed zero. The local axial flow is w=−U(1−y/h)+px​y(y−h)/(2μ), so its flux per circumference is −Uh/2−px​h3/(12μ)=−Q. Rearranging proves the displayed pressure gradient. A linear compliance p=p0​+α(r0​−r) couples this flow to deformation. Specified end pressures and zero net axial body force close the problem.

Force-free pressure drop of an annular lubrication plug (Δp=a2μ​∫(4U/h−6Q/h2)dx)

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Lubrication model of a compliant translating plug OurBigBook.com
The pressure force on a plug-and-film control volume is πa2Δp. Its opposing wall traction is 2πaμ∫wy​(0)dx, where wy​(0)=4U/h−6Q/h2. Equating them for a freely moving body proves the displayed formula. Writing s=2Q/U, h=sH and x=s/κ​X converts it into H(−L)−H(L)=Cλ∫[4/(3H)−1/H2]dX, with C=s/a and λ=6μU/(ακ​s5/2).
Small-speed compliant-plug lubrication asymptotics (b−2=32​(1−C)+O(C2),Δp∼8π2/3​μU/(aκs​))
Words: 63
Force-free pressure drop of an annular lubrication plug OurBigBook.com
For HX​+λ(H−2−H−3)=X, small λ gives H0​=(b2+X2)/2. In the large-domain limit its inverse-power integrals are I1​=2π/b, I2​=2π/b3 and I3​=3π/b5. The force-free condition is I2​−I3​=C(4I1​/3−I2​), or 2b2−3=C(8b4/3−2b2). Expanding the root near b−2=2/3 proves the displayed minus sign and leading pressure drop. The absolute downstream pressure relative to the elastic reference pressure fixes s and therefore closes the speed-pressure relation.

Annular inviscid-core displacement (u1​=Au0′​/(R+y),v1​=−Ax​u0​/(R+y))

Words: 169 Articles: 2
Physiological fluid dynamics OurBigBook.com
For a long, weak, axisymmetric indentation of an annular fully developed flow, use r=R+y and scale normal velocity by the inverse longitudinal scale ratio. The leading Euler equations for an inviscid fluid give zero longitudinal pressure gradient and u0​u1x​+v1​u0′​=0. Together with u1x​+(rv1​)y​/r=0, this yields ψ1​=Au0​, hence the displayed displacement fields. Thin viscous boundary layers enforce tangential wall conditions separately.

Forced annular displacement equation (σAxxx​−βα1​At​−α2​AAx​=βγ0​Ft​+γ02​FFx​+(γ02​/R)(AF)x​)

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Annular inviscid-core displacement OurBigBook.com
A distinguished annular indentation limit has λ−2=O(ϵ), λSt=O(ϵ) and Re≫λϵ−3. Define β=λSt/ϵ, σ=(λ2ϵ)−1∫01​u02​/(R+y)dy, α1​=γ0​/R+γ1​/(R+1) and α2​=γ02​/R2−γ12​/(R+1)2. Radial inertia supplies the pressure difference σAxx​ between the walls. The axial momentum limits and the moving-wall condition supply its derivative, giving the displayed forced KdV equation. This reduction assumes the viscous boundary layers remain thin and their displaced flux is smaller than O(ϵ2).
Opposite propagation directions in the annular displacement equation (ω=σk3/(βα1​),A=−3βα1​csech2(ks​ξ)/α2​)
Words: 52
Forced annular displacement equation OurBigBook.com
With no forcing, the linear dispersion relation has positive phase velocity σk2/(βα1​) and group velocity three times this. A decaying permanent wave with ξ=x+ct instead obeys σ(A′)2=A2(βα1​c+α2​A/3). For positive coefficients a nonzero homoclinic wave requires c>0 and is negative, travelling upstream. Its inverse width is ks​=21​βα1​c/σ​. The opposite directions reflect the nonlinear amplitude-dependent propagation speed.

Peristaltic pumping

Words: 105 Articles: 1
Physiological fluid dynamics OurBigBook.com
Peristaltic pumping transports fluid by a travelling deformation or travelling external pressure acting on a tube. With wave coordinate X=x−ct, mass conservation makes the relative flux Q=α(u−c) constant. The laboratory flux is αu=cα+Q, so a negative relative flux does not rule out forward mean pumping.

Weak peristaltic pumping of a collapsible tube (Q2​=2α0​c(n+1)​P0′2​+(R0​c/(kα0​))2Pe2​​)

A fluid is a material that flows under sustained shear and cannot maintain a static shear stress in its fluid state. Liquids and gases are the usual examples. A Newtonian fluid has deviatoric stress proportional to its rate of deformation, whereas more general fluid constitutive laws can be nonlinear or have memory. In a porous medium, the fluid occupies connected voids within a load-bearing solid framework.

In a closed tank of cross-sectional area S, entrainment into a uniform upper layer conserves the density deficit (ρl​−ρu​)h. Thus B=g′h is constant. With depth z increasing downward, gravitational potential energy is −gS∫0H​ρ(z)zdz=E∗​+ρl​SBh/2, so its rate of increase is proportional to the rate of deepening. This includes homogenization throughout the upper layer, not merely lifting a thin parcel across the interface.

Homogenization down to z=−d conserves buoyancy and gives mixed buoyancy b1​−[Δbd+N2d2/2]/(a+d). Integrating gravitational potential energy over the initial and final profiles gives the displayed increase per unit area. Its derivative is ρ0​[Δba/2+N2ad/2+N2d2/4]. Specifying absorbed mixing power is not enough to determine deepening unless the initial depth or an alternative upper-reservoir model is supplied.

Fixed-energy turbulent mixed layer (u2h=AΩ2R3)

Words: 176 Articles: 2
Fluid entrainment OurBigBook.com
In a slowly deepening mixed layer driven by a rotating boundary, a phenomenological balance between energy input, turbulent loss and acceleration of entrained fluid can keep total kinetic energy approximately fixed. For a tank of radius R this gives u2h=AΩ2R3, so velocity decreases as h−1/2. The closure does not make the speed constant and is an additional physical assumption rather than a direct consequence of mass conservation.

Natural ventilation

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Natural ventilation exchanges indoor and outdoor fluid through openings using pressure differences created by buoyancy or wind.

Ventilation after a heating reduction (xs​=1−x​−λ)

Words: 93
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
For an ideal two-layer natural ventilation transient following a heating change Q↦λQ, let V0​ and θ0​ be the initial flow and temperature excess, s=V0​t/(Ar​H), η=h/H, and x=η(1−θ/θ0​). The integrated buoyancy pressure gives V/V0​=1−x​, while heat balance gives xs​=1−x​−λ. A material interface satisfies ηs​=1−x​, so η=x+λs. For 0<λ<1, x increases toward 1−λ2 and ηs​≥λ, ensuring finite-time filling of the room. After filling, y=θ/θ0​ obeys ys​=λ−y3/2 and tends to λ2/3. This model assumes well-mixed individual layers, negligible wall heat capacity and a sharp advected interface.

Well-mixed ventilation temperature balance (Vθ˙=H−∣q∣θ)

Words: 200 Articles: 2
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
For a distributed heat source, a well-mixed interior with temperature excess θ gains temperature-volume flux H and loses ∣q∣θ by ventilation in either direction. With signed upward throughflow, q∣q∣=KA​(GT​θ±W), where GT​=gαT​Hb​ and W is wind pressure divided by mass density. The plus sign is assisting wind. Steady temperatures satisfy θ2(GT​θ+W)=H2/KA​ for assistance, or θ2∣GT​θ−W∣=H2/KA​ for opposition. Direction restrictions must be applied to roots.

Opposing-wind ventilation bistability (ε=GT​H/(KA​​W3/2))

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Well-mixed ventilation temperature balance OurBigBook.com
For 0<ε<2/(33​), the well-mixed ventilation temperature balance has one stable upward-flow temperature and two downward-flow temperatures. The heat-removal curve on the latter interval is KA​​θW−GT​θ​, maximal at 2W/(3GT​). Its lower-temperature root is stable and its higher-temperature root unstable. The two meet at a saddle-node bifurcation. The unstable root separates the basins of the stable wind-dominated and buoyancy-dominated states.
Ventilation switching under wind and heating changes
Words: 81
Opposing-wind ventilation bistability OurBigBook.com
Increasing wind or reducing heating both reduce the control parameter of opposing-wind ventilation bistability. However, wind moves the reversal threshold θw​=W/GT​, whereas heating does not. A sufficiently abrupt wind increase can place a hot upward-flow state in the cooler state's basin. Reducing positive heating at fixed wind cannot make an upward-flow state cross θw​, because its temperature time derivative there is positive. Slow variation follows a persistent stable branch; a fold destroys the cooler branch when wind is weakened or heat input increased.

Words: 69
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
An effective opening area may absorb both the discharge coefficient and the factor of two in an orifice law. If Ae​=2​Cd​Ageom​, its discharge is q=Ae​δp/ρ​. Two equal openings carrying the same flux share the total pressure drop, so q2=Ae2​Δp/(2ρ). They do not share equal drops when an internal volume source makes their fluxes unequal. State the effective-area convention before comparing numerical factors in natural ventilation models.

Displacement ventilation

Words: 557 Articles: 7
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
Displacement ventilation supplies relatively cool air at low level and removes warmer air at high level. In the ideal two-layer model, buoyant plumes feed a warm upper layer above a sharp density interface while the supply occupies the lower layer.

Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
For a pure plume with gp′​=γB2/3z−5/3, a steady sharp interface at zi​ has Qp​=B1/3zi5/3​/γ and warm-layer reduced gravity g′=B/Qp​. A freely discharging upper doorway of height D and width W has available head D−zi​. Equating plume supply to the broad-crested weir flux gives the displayed implicit height relation, with 0<zi​<D. Warm air above the doorway stores heat but adds no available head at its crest in this uniform-layer model.

Words: 80
Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
Two independent point-source pure plumes with ψ=B1​/B2​<1 remove lower-layer volume Q=C(B11/3​+B21/3​)h15/3​. If plume 1 feeds the middle layer, its reduced gravity is g1′​=B1​/[CB11/3​h15/3​]. The upper outflow carries both sources, so g2′​=(B1​+B2​)/Q, yielding the displayed ratio. Opening flow is driven by the integrated hydrostatic head g1′​(h2​−h1​)+g2′​(H−h2​). A plume crossing the lower interface has altered buoyancy relative to its new ambient and must be continued with nonzero incoming mass and momentum fluxes rather than reset as a zero-flux pure plume.

Source-volume blocking of displacement ventilation (Qc​=(Ae2​BH)1/3)

Words: 68
Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
A source volume Q makes roof outflow exceed floor inflow by Q. At zero floor inflow, an entraining plume cannot support a steady cold lower layer; the warm layer reaches the floor. With reduced gravity g′=B/Q, the entire hydrostatic head drives roof discharge Q=Ae​g′H​. This gives the stated threshold. Equal splitting of pressure head is inappropriate at blocking. The same result in physical-area notation is Qc​=(2Cd2​Ageom2​BH)1/3.

Ventilated filling-box relaxation (τh​,τb​)

Words: 71
Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
For total plume flux P(h), fixed ceiling exhaust F, zero ambient buoyancy, and uniform upper-layer reduced gravity b, the ideal two-layer balances are
Ah˙=F−P(h),dtd​[A(H−h)b]=B−Fb.
(62)
At P(h∗​)=F and b∗​=B/F, linearization yields the decay times τh​=A/P′(h∗​) and τb​=A(H−h∗​)/F. For P(h)∝h5/3, τh​=3Ah∗​/(5F). Upper-layer buoyancy relaxation usually dominates when h∗​≪H. Exact equilibrium is approached asymptotically; a fixed small relative tolerance takes order max(τh​,τb​)log(1/ε) after the initial transient.

No steady displacement layer without ambient supply

Words: 100
Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
Consider entraining plumes supplied with total source volume flux S, a separate lower-layer ambient inflow L, and ceiling exhaust F=S+L. Write P(h)=S+E(h), where E(h) is total fluid entrainment from the lower layer. Volume conservation gives Ah˙=L−E(h). A steady positive lower layer therefore requires L=E(h)>0. If L=0 and E(h)>0 for every h>0, no positive steady displacement-ventilation interface height exists. In a shifted pure plume approximation Pi​(h)=λBi1/3​(h+zi​)5/3 matched to source flux Si​ at h=0, this follows immediately from Pi​(h)>Si​ for h>0. This is a statement about the ideal two-layer model, not a prohibition of all possible stratification in a real ventilated room.

Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
Suppose n independent axisymmetric pure plumes share total buoyancy flux B equally, have negligible source volume flux, and are supplied with a separate ambient ventilation flux F at floor level. Their combined flux is P(h)=λn2/3B1/3h5/3. Volume conservation at a steady displacement-ventilation interface height and buoyancy flux conservation give
h∗​=(λn2/3B1/3F​)3/5,b∗​=FB​.
(63)
A positive two-layer state needs 0<h∗​<H, sources small relative to h∗​, and plumes sufficiently separated to remain independent. Splitting the sources increases total fluid entrainment and reduces the interface height by n−2/5. A finite source flux cannot simultaneously be neglected and supply all the replacement air; no steady displacement layer without ambient supply explains this restriction.

h=(3α2​)2/3B01/3​A​.

Single-opening exchange flow

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
A tall opening between fluids of different densities can support simultaneous inflow below a neutral pressure level and outflow above it. For a symmetric opening with a Boussinesq hydrostatic pressure difference and equal discharge coefficients, the neutral level lies at mid-height.

Neutral pressure level

Words: 24
Single-opening exchange flow OurBigBook.com
The neutral pressure level is the height at which indoor and outdoor hydrostatic pressures agree. Flow through an opening reverses direction across this level.

Stratified-room plume-exchange model

Words: 36
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
A stratified-room plume-exchange model balances the upward volume transported by a warm plume against downward transport by cold wall plumes. A global buoyancy balance relates the source flux to the buoyancy carried out through the vents.

A homologous spherical flow has velocity proportional to radius. Its velocity gradient is q(t)I and its velocity divergence is 3q(t).
